extracted.subtask_description: Norms and practical standards for newspaper editors and journalists: the personal qualities, professional knowledge, independence, accountability, and training the author argues are necessary for successful journalism and editorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility as an editorial advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: “it is the only profession in which versatility is not a disadvantage.” Specialism leads to perfection in some professions, but in journalism versatility is valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts other professions (law, medicine) where specialism yields excellence, arguing that in journalism breadth of capability across tasks is an asset rather than a liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to write and judge writing
rubrics_metrics.description: “The great editor is by no means the great writer. But he ought to be able to write and must be a judge of writing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An editor need not be the best creative writer, but must be able to write competently and judge the quality of others' writing when selecting, editing, or directing content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive knowledge of newspaper operations
rubrics_metrics.description: “The newspaper office is a little kingdom. The great editor needs to know and does know every range of it between the editorial room, the composing room and the pressroom.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An editor should 'hold well in hand everybody and every function,' ideally having risen step-by-step through the paper so as to understand all operational roles and technical processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced temperament and practical sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: He should be “level-headed, yet impressionable; sympathetic, yet self-possessed; able quickly to sift, detect and discriminate; of various knowledge, experience and interest.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clusters personal qualities: steadiness combined with responsiveness, sympathy tempered by self-possession, quick critical judgment, and wide-ranging knowledge and interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation, humility and devotion to the art (disinterestedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nothing too small for him to tackle, nothing too great, he should keep to the middle of the road... loving his art--for such it is--for art's sake; getting his sufficiency, along with its independence, in the public approval and patronage, seeking never anything further for himself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes avoiding extremes, seeking public trust rather than personal preferment, and loving journalism as an art rather than a means to personal aggrandizement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unselfishness and rejection of preferment/bribery
rubrics_metrics.description: “Disinterestedness being the soul of successful journalism, unselfish devotion to every noble purpose in public and private life, he should say to preferment, as to bribers, 'get behind me, Satan.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists/editors must resist offers of preferment and bribery, maintaining unselfish devotion to noble public purposes as foundational to credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visible accountability and trustworthiness (personal journalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Personal journalism cannot be escaped... the 'one-man power'... must be clear and answerable, responsive to the common weal, and, above all, trustworthy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the public expects a visible, answerable presence behind a paper, leaders of the press must be accountable and trustworthy; anonymity or hidden control undermines public confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to educate and distinguish wholesome from meretricious content
rubrics_metrics.description: “As the world passes... the daily journal is destined... to become the teacher--the very Bible--of the people. The people are already beginning to distinguish between the wholesome and the meretricious in their newspapers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers have an educative role and responsibility to the public to present wholesome, substantive material rather than sensational or meretricious fare; owners and editors must value character accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence from political servility
rubrics_metrics.description: “In my day newspaper independence was little known... Mr. Greeley was willing to play bottle-holder to Mr. Seward... Bennett challenged this kind of servility.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author presents independence from parties, politicians, and patronage as a core standard — editors should resist being instruments of political servility or private interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for training, perspective, and mastery of technical details (against stunt-chasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Too often the newspaper subaltern obtaining promotion... has failed to acquire even the most rudimentary knowledge of his art. He has been too busy seeking 'scoops' and doing 'stunts' to concern himself about perspectives, principles, causes and effects, probable impressions and consequences, or even to master the technical details which make such a difference in the preparation of matter intended for publication and popular perusal.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical training (e.g., journalism schools) and disciplined study are recommended to instill perspective, attention to consequences, principles, and the technical craft of preparing matter for publication, rather than prioritizing sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of formal schooling to set direction and foster independent judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: “The School of Journalism may not be always able to give him the needful instruction. But it can set him in the right direction and better prepare him to think and act for himself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not a complete substitute for experience, formal journalism education is portrayed as useful for orienting practitioners, teaching fundamentals, and encouraging independent critical thinking.
